title: Nexwall Firewall 26.0.0-rc1
summary: The first release candidate of Nexwall Firewall: Network Protection (IPS), Application Control, threat feeds, geo-blocking, a log viewer with live rule tracing, a faster data path and a licensing model delivered from signed Nexwall services.
overview:
Nexwall Firewall 26.0.0-rc1 is the first release candidate of the Nexwall firewall. It is an installable image for x86-64 machines and virtual machines, with a web interface in English, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese.

The protection features are served by Nexwall: intrusion signatures, the application catalog and the threat lists are built on Nexwall servers, signed, checked by the firewall and refreshed every day. Updates of the web interface and of the license component come from a signed Nexwall feed whose files are pinned by checksum.

This is a release candidate. Use it to evaluate, to test in the lab and to give feedback; do not use it as the only protection of a production network yet.

sections.title: What is new
sections.intro: The features below are new in this release.

items.title: Guided setup
items.body: The first start guides you through everything a new firewall needs: the administrator password, the name of the firewall, how it connects to the internet (automatic DHCP by default, fixed IP address or PPPoE), remote access and the security services. After the setup the firewall protects the network without further configuration.
bullets: The WAN interface and the address it received are shown during the setup.
The default name is FIREWALL.
The security services are switched on by default; the countries or regions to block are chosen on the last pages.
A language icon on every page, also on the login page, changes the language and the choice is remembered.
Nothing is applied until you finish the setup.

items.title: Network Protection (IPS)
items.body: Inline intrusion prevention that inspects forwarded traffic and blocks attacks before they reach your servers and users. The page that was called IPS / IDS is now Network Protection (IPS), and the default action for detected threats is Block. You can switch to Detect only and turn alert logging on or off.
bullets: The signature bundle combines three sources in policy tiers: the Snort community rules (4,017 rules), a converted open rule set (51,873 rules) and rules written by Nexwall Labs. It is built on Nexwall servers, signed, and refreshed daily.
The firewall verifies every bundle, validates it with Snort before installing it and rolls back to the previous one if it does not load.
A signatures card shows the bundle in use and lets you update it on demand.
Queues and analysis threads follow the number of CPU cores.
When the license no longer allows the service, the page shows a banner and inspection is suspended instead of failing silently.
items.note: Signature updates need a license; the trial includes them. The open sources used are redistributed under their own licenses.

items.title: Application Control (DPI)
items.body: Recognizes the applications and services crossing the firewall and lets you block, re-prioritize or report them. The traffic classification engine is Netify Agent 5.2.8 with Nexwall's own plugins, and enforcement is applied in the firewall as nftables rules that are validated before they replace the running ones.
bullets: A Nexwall application catalog is delivered daily. The first build knew about 1,500 applications with about 26,000 domain rules, 783 network rules and 26 soft dissectors, compared with 199 applications in the open list shipped with the engine, so far fewer flows stay Unknown.
A Settings tab shows the catalog status and lets you update now or choose the automatic update frequency.
Rules can act on a single application or on a whole category.

Enforcement is tied to a short-lived feature token from the license service. If the token cannot be renewed, enforcement is suspended within seconds and a banner says so; it resumes when the service is back.
Traffic statistics per application are available while the license is active.

items.title: Threat Shield feeds
items.body: Nexwall now builds and serves its own block lists. A firewall downloads them from Nexwall, checks the signature and the checksum of every file and applies them locally, instead of reading lists from third-party servers.
bullets: Twelve DNS categories, about 3.2 million entries in total: advertising and tracking, adult content, filter bypass, crypto mining, drugs, gambling, malware (core and extended), phishing, piracy, ransomware and scams.
Two IP lists: known attackers and botnet command servers.
Each list shows a readable title, the number of entries and a confidence level, so you can decide what to switch on.
The lists are rebuilt every day; the firewall checks every 30 minutes and reloads its DNS service only when something changed.
A sensible set of categories is switched on by default and your own choices are kept when you update. A selection made with the earlier categories is migrated.
items.note: The Nexwall lists need a license; the trial includes them. They are built only from sources whose licenses allow redistribution.

items.title: Memory warning for DNS lists
items.body: Large lists need memory. The DNS block lists page now shows how much memory the switched-on categories need compared with the memory installed, and warns you when they would use more than a fifth of it (an error above a third).
bullets: As a guide, every blocked domain takes about 75 bytes.

items.title: Geo-blocking from Nexwall servers
items.body: Country blocking now uses address lists built by Nexwall from the public registry allocation data (five regional internet registries), split by country and published in the same signed bundle as the other lists. The firewall loads them from local files in seconds, instead of downloading a list per country every time the service starts.
bullets: IPv4 (about 179,000 blocks) and IPv6 (about 70,000 blocks) are covered.
Registry data shows where an address block was allocated, not always where it is used today.

items.title: Log Viewer
items.body: A new viewer for the firewall's logs, opened from the Logs page in its own window. Logs are stored locally for 30 days and the viewer follows the interface language and theme.
bullets: Thirteen tabs: firewall, IP and geo blocking, intrusion prevention, application control, DNS filtering, VPN, high availability, reverse proxy, authentication, administrator activity, system and more.
Every blocked line tells you the reason; a rule with logging turned on is logged under its own name.
Click a value to filter by it, and export the result to CSV.
Live rule tracing shows which rule accepted, rejected or dropped a packet, including blocks by application control; the trace link on each firewall row starts it.
The viewer runs only while it is enabled.

items.title: Fast path and performance settings
items.body: Established connections that need no inspection can bypass most of the packet processing. The fast path is selective: traffic that Network Protection or Application Control must see stays on the inspected path, and connection counters keep working. It is off by default and is one switch on both the Application Control and Network Protection settings pages.
bullets: Packet steering spreads network processing across the CPU cores; it is on by default for new multi-core installations.
Larger network card buffers are on by default for new installations. Small default buffers dropped bursts in tests.
The connection tracking table scales with installed memory (32 entries per MiB, at least 65,536).
Application Control instances are sized from the CPU count (half of the cores, one to four); Network Protection uses one thread per CPU.

items.title: Engine monitor
items.body: A new page shows what the inspection engines are doing: how busy the traffic classification and intrusion prevention engines are and how much load they put on the machine. Use it to see whether a machine is sized correctly.

items.title: Stalled inspection watchdog
items.body: If an inspection queue stops issuing verdicts, new connections would wait forever. A watchdog checks every minute, detects a stuck or badly backed-up queue, writes a report with the details, logs it and restarts the engine that owns the queue. The longest outage before recovery is about one to two minutes.

items.title: Licensing
items.body: A firewall registers itself with the license server: no code is typed. It starts in a 30-day trial that includes Application Control, Network Protection, DNS Filtering, IP & Geo Blocking and VPN Extended, and the trial ends when your reseller applies a subscription. The Licensing page lists the subscriptions that are active and the ones that are not, including the additional Web Server Protection (WAF) and Email Protection (MTA), and has a Synchronize with server button. The license component updates itself from the signed feed and downloads large data sets reliably.

items.title: Signed update feed
items.body: The web interface, the license component and the traffic-engine plugins are published to a signed Nexwall feed. Every file is pinned by its SHA-256 checksum in the firmware build, so an image always contains exactly the version it was built with.

items.title: Also in the image
items.body: The firewall platform includes the functions you expect from a complete firewall.
bullets: Zones, policies, port forwarding, NAT, multiple WAN with failover and QoS.
VPN: IPsec tunnels and OpenVPN remote access, both tested in this release.
Authentication against a remote Active Directory, tested in this release.
High availability, reverse proxy with certificates, captive portal and DNS category filtering through a cloud resolver.
Monitoring with real-time graphs and Checkmk checks, configuration backup and central management.

items.title: Unit name in the top bar
items.body: The name of the firewall is shown at the right of the top bar, next to the Log Viewer button.

items.title: Enable all lists at once
items.body: The DNS Filtering and the IP & Geo Blocking pages have an Enable all switch at the top right of the lists. A new firewall switches all the Nexwall lists on by itself when they arrive, if its memory allows it.

items.title: Sensible firewall defaults
items.body: A new installation no longer starts with an empty forward rules list. It starts with two rules: LAN -> WAN, which allows your internal networks to reach the internet, and DROP DEFAULT, which closes that path and logs what it drops.
bullets: DROP DEFAULT cannot be deleted or moved; it always stays the last forward rule.
A rule you add is placed above it automatically, so it takes effect.
items.note: Existing firewalls keep their current configuration.

items.title: Clearer output rules
items.body: The description of output rules now says what they are: rules for traffic that the firewall itself starts, such as updates, DNS, license checks and VPN connections. Every zone already allows this traffic, so you only need output rules to restrict it.

items.title: Web interface
items.body: The interface carries the Nexwall design and is available in English, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese; tabs follow the chosen language. The Threat Shield tables show titles, entry counts and confidence for every list, and the pages for the licensed features say clearly when a license is missing.

items.title: Accurate traffic figures
items.body: The traffic shown in the Monitor (daily traffic, top talkers, live flows) now matches the interface counters. In a test with a 36 MB download the Monitor showed 35.99 MB against 36.33 MB on the interface; before it showed 14 KB.

items.title: Nexwall naming and services
items.body: The product, the image file names, the host name (Nexwall) and the service endpoints use Nexwall names. Registration, inventory, backup, telemetry, updates and licenses are served from Nexwall hosts.

items.title: No third-party list mirrors
items.body: Threat Shield no longer reads block lists from third-party servers or from a mirror. Everything comes from the signed Nexwall bundle.

items.title: Reinstalled firewall stayed unregistered
items.body: A firewall that was reinstalled kept its old registration on the license server and could not get its license or its downloads (IPS signatures, lists). Your reseller can now reset the device in the license panel, and the firewall registers again by itself.

items.title: Log Viewer did not open
items.body: Opening the Log Viewer restarted the web server under the request that asked for it and the browser reported a network error. Enabling it again no longer restarts anything, and the first time the page waits for the web server.

items.title: DNS & DHCP page failed to load
items.body: The page raised an error when an interface address was stored as 192.168.1.1/24. Addresses are now read in every form and interfaces without a usable IPv4 address are skipped.

items.title: Traffic engine crash loop
items.body: A plugin of the traffic engine crashed the engine again and again right after it started. The cause was found with a symbolized backtrace and fixed.

items.title: Engine using a whole CPU core
items.body: A plugin queue spun without waiting and kept the engine at 100% of a core. It now waits for work like the other plugins.

items.title: Engine deadlock
items.body: A plugin could lock the engine against itself. The call path was changed so the engine no longer blocks.

items.title: Large license data downloads
items.body: Downloads of big data sets from the license service were cut silently at 1 MiB and timed out after 30 seconds. They now accept up to 64 MiB and have ten minutes to complete.

items.title: Memory exhaustion with very high connection limits
items.body: A fixed, very high connection tracking limit could exhaust memory on small machines under heavy load. The limit is now derived from the installed memory.

items.title: Bursts dropped on virtual network cards
items.body: Small default network card buffers dropped traffic bursts and kept throughput low in tests. Larger buffers and packet steering are now on by default for new installations.

components.intro: The versions below make up the image. Most of them are pinned by checksum, so the image always contains exactly these versions. The signature bundle, the application catalog and the threat lists are not part of the image: they are downloaded and refreshed daily.

timeline.intro: How this release came together, from the first image to the release candidate.

entries.title: First image
entries.text: Nexwall branding, naming and licensing files; the baseline image booted in a virtual machine.

entries.title: Nexwall sources
entries.text: The web interface, monitoring, captive portal and Checkmk checks are built from Nexwall repositories; Application Control enforcement and its statistics were added; services moved to Nexwall hosts; the DNS & DHCP address bug was fixed.

entries.title: First Nexwall-only image
entries.text: Booted with the new interface and Portuguese translation; an IPsec tunnel to a third-party firewall, a remote Active Directory and OpenVPN remote access were configured and worked.

entries.title: Traffic engine 5.2.8 and Nexwall plugins
entries.text: The engine was upgraded and the flow, statistics and HTTP-sink plugins were verified end to end on a running unit.

entries.title: Application Control actions
entries.text: The action plugin was tested live; a crash loop and a busy-wait that used a whole CPU core were found and fixed, and labels were confirmed end to end.

entries.title: Catalog, accounting and logs
entries.text: The Nexwall application catalog, the traffic accounting fix, the Log Viewer with live rule tracing and the stalled-queue watchdog were built and tested.

entries.title: Signed feed and licensed services
entries.text: The signed update feed, feature tokens for Application Control, statistics and Network Protection, the intrusion signature service and the Network Protection gate plugin.

entries.title: Performance, threat feeds and defaults
entries.text: Inspection threads, fast path, packet steering, larger buffers and the Engine monitor; Network Protection naming and Block default; daily refresh of signatures and catalog; Threat Shield feeds, geo-blocking and the memory warning; the default firewall rules; web interface 1.3.6; the release candidate image.

entries.title: Guided setup and licensing by module
entries.text: Setup wizard with network and security steps, subscriptions by module, registration without a code, enable-all switches, Log Viewer fix, web interface 1.3.7 and license component 1.6.0.

known_issues.title: New defaults apply to new installations only
known_issues.body: The LAN -> WAN and DROP DEFAULT rules, packet steering and larger network card buffers are part of the default configuration. A firewall installed earlier keeps the settings it has.
known_issues.workaround: Add the two rules by hand on an existing firewall and keep DROP DEFAULT at the end of the list.

known_issues.title: Reinstalled firewalls
known_issues.body: A firewall that is reinstalled while it is assigned to a customer needs its device reset by the reseller before it can get its license again.

known_issues.title: Additional subscriptions
known_issues.body: Web Server Protection (WAF) and Email Protection (MTA) are listed as subscriptions, but their features are not available yet.

known_issues.title: Country blocking without a license
known_issues.body: A firewall without a license cannot use the Nexwall country lists. Country blocking then uses the public lists of the underlying component, which are downloaded every time the service starts and can take a long time.

known_issues.title: Large DNS list selections
known_issues.body: Reloading the DNS service with about 1.8 million blocked domains interrupts name resolution for roughly ten seconds. Lists are reloaded only when they change, normally once a day.
known_issues.workaround: Switch off the categories you do not need. The memory warning on the DNS block lists page helps you choose.

known_issues.title: Emulated network cards limit throughput
known_issues.body: In virtual machines with emulated Intel e1000 network cards, throughput stays around 0.7 to 1 Gbit/s whatever the CPU. This is a limit of the emulation, not of the firewall.
known_issues.workaround: Use paravirtualized adapters (virtio or vmxnet3) or physical hardware for performance tests.

known_issues.title: Fast path is off by default
known_issues.body: The fast path has been verified for correctness and counters, but it has not been measured on physical hardware yet.
known_issues.workaround: Switch it on in the Performance card of the Application Control or Network Protection settings and compare on your own traffic.

known_issues.title: Encrypted traffic
known_issues.body: Application Control and Network Protection do not decrypt HTTPS. Applications are recognized from the connection, the domain name and the traffic pattern.

known_issues.title: Release candidate
known_issues.body: Interfaces and defaults can still change before the final release.

requirements: x86-64 processor, UEFI firmware with Secure Boot off.
At least two network interfaces (one for the internal network, one for the internet).
2 GB of memory with the default threat categories; 4 GB or more if you switch on the adult, advertising and extended malware lists.
Internet access to updates.nexwall.com.br, license.nexwall.com.br and services.nexwall.com.br for updates, licenses, threat feeds and registration.
upgrade: The release is an installable disk image for virtual machines and appliances. Check its SHA-256 first.
After the first start the internal interface answers on 192.168.1.1. Change the administrator password on the first login.
Firewalls running an earlier internal build are not upgraded in place by this release candidate; install the image on a test machine and compare.
Do not restore a configuration backup taken on an older internal build: its traffic engine settings use another format.
To check the file on Linux run sha256sum on it; on Windows run Get-FileHash with -Algorithm SHA256 in PowerShell. The result must equal the SHA-256 in the Downloads table.
The administration guide is at https://docs.nexwall.com.br.
open_source: Nexwall Firewall is built on open source software, among them OpenWrt, the Linux kernel, nftables, Snort 3, Netify Agent and nDPI, dnsmasq, banIP, adblock and VictoriaMetrics. The firewall and the operator tools are published under their original licenses, and the license texts and notices are shipped with the image and available on request. The Threat Shield lists are built from open sources whose licenses allow redistribution, and the notice that lists them is part of every bundle.
